newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian bank merger to shake up construction.
newsitem.headline: Austrian bank merger to shake up construction.

text.p: The European Commission's approval of the merger of Austria's two top banks has ended upheaval in the financial sector but could trigger a major shift in the building industry, analysts said on Wednesday.
The Commission gave the green light to Bank Austria's acquisition of Creditanstalt on condition the new bank reduced its interests in several areas, including construction.
Bank Austria must either sell its 50 percent stake in STUAG AG or Creditanstalt's 80 percent of shares in Universale Bau AG. Analysts rated STUAG the most likely sale candidate.
"Bank Austria is in a comfortable position. It can do something it has already agreed to -- sell its stake STUAG," said a Vienna-based analyst who declined to be named.
He forecast that Bank Austria would try to convince Strabag Oesterreich AG, a unit of Germany's Strabag AG, to exercise a five-year buy-out option for STUAG early.

Bank Austria and Strabag each bought 50 percent of STUAG in September 1995, putting Strabag-STUAG firmly at the top of Austrian construction with combined sales of about 18 billion schillings ($1.5 billion) annually.
Strabag and Bank Austria declined to comment on the speculation. Bank Austria spokesman Heimo Hackl noted the bank was under no time pressure to implement the European Commission's decision.

"I think we will have plenty of time and that we will not be forced into a last minute deal," he said, adding that it was conceivable that Bank Austria's existing commitment to sell STUAG after five years would satisfy the commission.
The likelihood of a STUAG sale has not prevented Austria's second biggest construction group Bau Holding from showing an interest in the second potential sell-off candidate, Universale.
"Basically we are interested but it depends on the conditions," Bau Holding board member Hannes Truntschnig said.

A strict cost-cutting programme in the wake of deep losses in 1993 and 1994 bore fruit for Universale in 1995 when the firm returned to the black. Last year it achieved a turnover of around 7.3 billion schillings and a pre-tax profit of 30 million, according to preliminary figures.
Analysts forecast foreign companies might join a race for Universale. "Such a big company can not be sold without a tender and I would expect some foreign interest," said one.

Others said Bank Austria might consider consolidating its construction interests by selling STUAG then merging Universale with Allgemeine Bau A. Porr, in which it has a stake of roughly a third. Bank Austria's Hackl declined to comment the speculation. ($ = 12.03 Austrian Schillings)
